newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea to give 50,000 tonnes of corn to North.
newsitem.headline: South Korea to give 50,000 tonnes of corn to North.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross Society reached agreement with its counterpart from rival Pyongyang on Friday to provide 50,000 tonnes of corn to the hungry North.

"The North Korean side said they are satisfied with the amount," Lee Byoung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross Society, told reporters after the signing of the agreement that followed three days of talks in Beijing.

While the South rejected a request from the North for rice as well as the corn because of disagreement over transparency of distribution, the two sides did agree on greater access for monitoring by the International Federation of Red Cross (IFRC) and Red Crescent Societies.

The value of the second batch of food aid from the Southern side was put at $10 million and the corn was to be delivered by the end of September, Lee said. A first amount was agreed last May with delivery to be completed by the end of this month.
The latest aid would be delivered in three shipments by land and two by sea with most of the grain to be sourced in China, South Korean officials said.

International aid workers say the communist North is on the brink of famine after floods in 1995 and 1996 devastated much of the country's farmland and industrial bases, exacerbating already severe food shortages.
Pyongyang has said severe drought is threatening to do even more damage to its agricultural sector this year.
Aid workers have said more such talks between the Red Cross societies of the two rival Koreas could not be ruled out if North Korea fails to reap a good harvest this year.
"The two sides expressed hope for a good harvest in October and hoped this could be the last delivery," Lee said.
He said the Northern side was content even though the South turned down their request for rice, which can be stored for longer than corn, amid disagreement over transparency.
The Southern side had been pushing for a deal that would designate individual families for food relief and allow South Korean reporters to monitor deliveries. The North refused.
"We could not achieve this because of objections from North Korea," Lee said.
However, North Korea had agreed to allow the IFRC to expand its monitoring operations beyond the 19 counties where it is currently allowed to work in the Stalinist, hermit nation.

"The North Korean side shall guarantee that the IFRC in North Korea can confirm the result of the distribution of materials," Lee said. "This means this time we will strengthen the role of the IFRC in North Korea."
An IFRC official said it needed to hold more talks.
"We are willing to carry out these requests but it will require further negotiations with the North," said IFRC regional delegation head Johan Schaar.
Schaar, an observer to the talks, said North Korea needed 10,000 tonnes of grain a month to feed 740,000 people on the basis of 450 grammes (15 ounces) per day.
The aid agreed last May came on top of $16 million worth of donations made by Seoul in response to an appeal by the U.N. World Food Programme.
Washington also this month nearly doubled its total food aid to North Korea to $52 million, intended to combat widespread malnutrition, particularly among children.
